references.text: The fourth commandment concerning the Sabbath, which states that six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord.
Repeats the command to work six days and rest on the seventh day.
Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest, even during plowing time and harvest time.
Repeats almost word for word the same message about the Sabbath as a holy day of rest and the death penalty for those who work.
The Sabbath is described as a holy assembly and a complete day of rest.
An example of the death penalty for breaking the Sabbath, where a man is stoned for gathering wood on the Sabbath.
The restatement of the Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy.
Ezekiel refers to the Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel, set apart for the Lord.
Jesus discusses the meaning of the Sabbath and declares that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
The Jews persecute Jesus because he healed on the Sabbath, sparking a discussion about work on the Sabbath.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people, with reference to resting from one's own works.
Explains the social and ethical reasoning behind the Sabbath commandment by extending the right to rest to the entire community.
Places the Sabbath commandment at the center of God's covenant and shows its role as a fundamental relationship between God and humanity.
Demonstrates that the Sabbath was a practical reality and God's gift before it was given as law with punishment.
It provides the creative basis for the Sabbath; showing that the law is built on God's own rest.
